title: 500 Snails Take an Overnight Flight to Tahiti to Rebuild Their Wild Population
summary:
Staff at the St. Louis Zoo recently opened a very special delivery: an overnight shipment of 500 adult Partula snails. The tiny invertebrates began their journey at the Detroit Zoo in Royal Oak, Michigan, and their final destination is Tahiti, where they will be released into the wild. It is part of an international effort to reestablish wild populations of Partula snails.

Partula snails are small, tree-dwelling creatures native to islands in French Polynesia. In Polynesian cultural heritage, each unique Partula shell represents an island. But when humans introduced the predatory rosy wolf snail to the region to control another invasive snail species, it devastated Partula populations. For decades, the Detroit Zoo has been breeding and raising Partula snails and helping return them to their native habitat by the thousands.

The 500 snails currently en route were all bred at the Detroit Zoo. Each shell features an orange dot of animal-safe paint that glows in UV light, identifying it as one of the snails released in 2026. Each year gets a different color, and the dots allow conservationists to monitor the snails in their natural habitat.

"The snails are sent 'priority overnight' via either FedEx or UPS," says Mark Vassallo, Curator of Amphibians at the Detroit Zoological Society. "The snails are carefully packed using insulating materials and special 'phase change' packs to stabilize the temperature inside. Currently the Detroit Zoological Society bred snails are taking a pit-stop at St. Louis Zoo where they will be fed a special diet in order to prepare them for the wild."

This upcoming release is part of a program that has returned 11 different Partula species formerly deemed extinct in the wild to their native environments, consisting of over 17,000 individual snails. The Audubon Nature Institute in New Orleans also recently sent 200 Partula snails to Tahiti.

When asked what success looks like, Vassallo explains that it can be defined in stages, but ultimately it means "a self-sustaining population with consistent reproduction and very importantly, proper habitat that is protected to sustain that species to allow long term recovery and stabilization of that population."
why_it_matters: The story shows how fragile island ecosystems are and how long repair takes: a single introduction in the 1970s can require decades of breeding programmes, overnight air freight and UV paint dots to undo. It is also a live test of the choice this generation faces — which species get rescued, which habitats get protected, and whether a repaired ecosystem can ever run on its own.

background_read: Partula snails are small, tree-dwelling snails that lived across the islands of French Polynesia (a group of islands in the South Pacific that is a territory of France), and each island's snails had shells so distinct that Polynesian tradition links them to the islands themselves.

In the 1970s and 1980s, officials introduced the rosy wolf snail — a fast, predatory snail from the Americas — to control the giant African land snail, a crop pest that had itself been introduced. Instead of solving the problem, the predator hunted the much smaller native Partula, and many species vanished within about a decade.

As wild numbers collapsed, zoos such as the Detroit Zoo and London Zoo joined an international Partula breeding programme, keeping 'insurance populations' in captivity — for some Partula species, zoos are now the only place they exist.
The IUCN Red List, the global catalogue of species at risk, lists a number of Partula species as extinct in the wild, an official category meaning they survive only in human care.

Reintroductions to the islands have been going on for years, but a release only counts as a success if the snails breed and survive without constant help — the same test faced by recovery programmes for species such as the California condor.

perspectives.description: Conservationists see one of the great zoo success stories: 11 species declared extinct in the wild are alive again on their home islands, and 500 more snails flying overnight shows the programme's seriousness. The colour-coded dots turn each release into real data about survival in the wild.

Critics of the original intervention point out that people caused this disaster: the rosy wolf snail was introduced to solve a pest problem and wiped out native species instead. A release programme, however careful, is a repair job — and the ecosystem may never return to exactly what it was.

Biologically, this tests the idea of 'insurance populations' — keeping a species alive in captivity until its habitat can be made safe. It has worked for species like the California condor, but it is expensive, slow, and realistic only for small creatures that breed well in zoos.

The final stage is whether the snails persist without human help. That depends less on zoos than on managing the islands' remaining predators, invasive plants and land pressures so a population can breed on its own — exactly the 'self-sustaining population' in protected habitat that Vassallo describes.
